content: Materials from low-risk areas can be temporarily stored, with the size of the storage area depending on the care facility. However, it is generally advisable to allocate a larger area due to the volume of items requiring storage. Tents that are intact and not made of absorbable materials can be stored for future reuse. Wooden shelters and fencing constructed with tarpaulin should be dismantled and burned due to their likely deteriorated condition. Concrete surfaces requiring demolition should be left until the end of the process to allow for the safe use of excavators. If manual demolition of concrete is necessary, precautions must be taken to prevent health and safety hazards. No equipment or materials should be abandoned on-site without approval from relevant regulatory authorities and affected landholders. If masonry or concrete structures are buried, responsible agencies should provide a site plan to the landowner and explain the location of the abandoned facilities. For buried and decommissioned latrine pits or septic tanks, a simple risk assessment should be conducted, considering factors such as soil type, water table, hydraulic gradient, and the time elapsed since the pit was buried. Repurposing Principles Key technical principles for repurposing an Ebola care facility include: The location and intended purpose of the structure. The quality of construction and materials used, especially for temporary structures. Evaluation of the water system in terms of quantity (especially during the dry season) and quality (with a focus on microbial containment). The quality and functionality of sanitation facilities. If permanent structures are to be returned to their original condition, an assessment of the building's condition should be performed, and maintenance activities should be completed before reopening. Reporting A final report on the decommissioning process should be submitted within two weeks of completion. This report should include: A completed checklist approved by an IPC officer and the Ministry of Health (MOH) or relevant authority and facility manager. A list of materials and equipment for reuse or donation. Site plans, including underground masonry or concrete structures, water points, and waste disposal areas (e.g., burn pits, latrine pits). Waste management processes. A photo journal. Conclusions and recommendations. A strategy for after-action review. Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) Principles for Terminal Cleaning and Decontamination Evidence suggests that the Ebola virus is relatively fragile, with its infectivity declining rapidly outside its host. It is highly susceptible to disinfectants such as chlorine, ethanol, and ultraviolet light. Key IPC principles for terminal cleaning and decontamination include: A trained IPC officer should inspect the facility before, during, and after cleaning and decontamination and supervise the process. A checklist of necessary cleaning and decontamination steps should be developed and used. Appropriate hand hygiene stations and areas for PPE donning and doffing should be established. Cleaners trained in safe cleaning practices should be briefed before starting. Staff health and safety should be monitored, and any injuries or illnesses reported. The facility should not be reopened for repurposing until the process is safely completed, documented, and signed off by the IPC officer. Visual improvements, such as repainting walls, landscaping, and refreshing furniture, may enhance the facility's acceptability and appeal for its new purpose. PPE for Terminal Cleaning In high-risk (red) zones, cleaners should wear full PPE as per WHO recommendations, including double gloves, a disposable gown or coverall, a waterproof apron, eye protection, and rubber boots. In low-risk (green) zones, lower-level PPE (disposable gown, heavy-duty gloves, mask, face shield, and boots) may be used. If no clear distinction exists between red and green zones, full PPE should be worn at all times. General Cleaning Instructions Cleaning should precede the application of disinfectants to prevent inactivation by organic matter. Cleaning and disinfectant solutions should be freshly prepared daily and changed every 2-3 hours during use. Cleaning should progress from clean to dirty areas to avoid cross-contamination. Dry sweeping and shaking out rags should be avoided to prevent the spread of virus particles. Use moistened cloths instead. All waste generated during cleaning should be disposed of in leak-proof plastic bags, collected in covered bins designated as infectious waste, and incinerated. Decontamination of Medical Devices and Equipment Medical devices should be cleaned, disinfected, and/or sterilized according to the manufacturer's instructions. In the absence of specific instructions, generic standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be followed. Medical assets should be categorized and decontaminated based on their design and complexity, with special attention to sharp-edged tools and electro-mechanical components. Water and Sanitation Facility Decontamination Temporary latrines should be disinfected, dismantled, and disposed of by incineration, burning, or deep burial. Pits should be backfilled with soil or solid debris and marked with signage and GPS coordinates. Permanent latrines should be cleaned and disinfected, with the process verified and approved by the MOH or designated authority before reuse. Septic tanks should be emptied only if more than two-thirds full, following national guidelines. If dismantled, inspection chambers should be sealed with concrete. Solid Waste Management Items that cannot be burned should be deep-buried at an approved site. All items must be decontaminated before disposal. Burning pits should be closed with one meter of soil after use, and all final waste disposal site coordinates should be logged with the MOH.
